paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.29:1 Rule 10.29 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.29. 1. General rule In Weatherford Canada Partnership v. Artemis Kautschuk and Kunstoff-Technik GmbH, 2019 ABCA 92, 2019 CarswellAlta 422, the Court said: [11] The discretion to award costs must be exercised judicially and in line with the factors in r 10.33: Stewart Estate v TAQA North Limited, 2016 ABCA 144 (CanLII) at para 26, 35 Alta LR (6th). The general rule is that costs are awarded on a party and party basis, and that this should represent partial indemnification of the successful party—approximately 40–50% of actual costs: Trizec Equities Ltd v Ellis-Don Management Services Ltd, 1999 ABQB 801 (CanLII) at para 20–21, 251 AR 101; Blaze Energy Ltd v Imperial Oil Resources, 2014 ABQB 509 (CanLII) at para 68, [2014] AJ No 916 (QL). [12] Party and party costs balance two competing interests: the unfairness of requiring a successful party whose conduct is not blameworthy to bear any costs and the chilling effect on parties bringing or defending claims if the unsuccessful party is required to bear all the costs: LSI Logic Corporation of Canada, Inc v Logani, 2001 ABQB 968 (CanLII) at para 5, [2002] 4 WWR 531 (LSI Logic). The result of this balance is the concept of partial indemnification through party and party costs to the successful party. [13] While costs are always in the discretion of the court, the cases recognize that when the litigation is complex and the amount at stake in the action in dispute greatly exceeds column 5, courts may award a multiplier of column 5 to help achieve the level of indemnification appropriate for party and party costs: Rocky Mountain House at para 13. To do so is not an error in principle. [14] An award of solicitor and client costs will be rare and must be based on a finding of intentional misconduct during the litigation. LSI Logic at paras 5–6; Luft v Taylor, Zinkhofer & Conway, 2017 ABCA 228 (CanLII) at para 75, 53 Alta LR (6d) 44 (Luft). Solicitor and client costs indemnify for costs that arise within the four corners of the litigation. Full indemnification costs, also known as solicitor and own client costs, compensate for services that are not strictly essential to the litigation. LSI Logic at para 4; Luft at para 77. They are “virtually unheard of” except when provided for by contract: Luft at para 78. Paragraph 14 of Weatherford was quoted with approval in Lotoski v. Lotoski, 2019 ABCA 262, 2019 CarswellAlta 1267 (at paragraph 3). In Norris v. Norris, 2024 ABKB 600, Justice Renke gave this summary of the law relating to the awarding of costs: [25] The Court of Appeal has recently provided guidance respecting costs determinations in cases including McAllister v Calgary (City), 2021 ABCA 25; Barkwell v McDonald, 2023 ABCA 87 (Barkwell 1); Barkwell v McDonald, 2023 ABCA 183 (Barkwell 2); Sunridge Nissan v McRuer, 2023 ABCA 128 at para 57; Petroupoulos v Petropoulos, 2023 ABCA 193, Pentelechuk JA; Kantor v Kantor, 2023 ABCA 329; VLM v Dominey Estate, 2023 ABCA 382; and Vaillancourt v Carter, 2024 ABCA 65. For background discussions, see (e.g.) GO Community Centre v Clark Builders and Stantec Consulting Ltd, 2020 ABQB 203 at paras 56-163; Ehli v Lamanator Coatings Ltd, 2024 ABKB 339; Grimes v Governors of the University of Lethbridge, 2023 ABKB 432, Graesser J, passim; Serinus Energy PLC v SysGen Solutions Group Ltd, 2024 ABKB 123, Marion J at paras 10-27; AGS v RNS, 2024 ABKB 280, Eamon J at paras 24-50; Prevatt v Prevatt, 2024 ABKB 386, DJ Reed J at paras 13-26. [26] Under r 10.29(1), a successful party is generally entitled to a costs award: McAllister at para 21; Serinus Energy at para 11. This is to say that the unsuccessful party is generally obligated to pay costs to the successful party. [27] Generally again, on the Alberta approach to costs, the unsuccessful party is not obligated to pay the full legal fees actually incurred by the successful party: McAllister at paras 37, 41; Barkwell 1 at para 58; VLM v Dominey Estate at para 4; AGS v RNS at para 30; Serinus Energy at para 24; RVB Managements Ltd v Rocky Mountain House (Town), 2015 ABCA 304 at para 14; Trizec Equities Limited v Ellis-Don Management Services Ltd, 1999 ABQB 801, Mason J at para 21. [28] The costs determination is “discretionary,” but not unfettered. The discretion must be exercised judicially. The discretion remains governed by principle, the rules and authorities: Styles v Caravan Trailer Lodges of Alberta Limited, 2019 ABQB 558, Jones J at para 47; Grimes v UofL at para 51; Stewart Estate v TAQA North Ltd, 2017 ABCA 144 at para 26; Vaillancourt v Carter at para 24; Serinus Energy at para 10. [29] But how is the amount of costs to be gauged? 1. Proportionality [30] The overarching principle is proportionality: Barkwell 1 at para 57; VLM v Dominey Estate at para 9; Petropoulos at para 18; Serinus Energy at para 27; Goldstick Estates (Re), 2019 ABCA 508 at para 31. Costs should reasonably indemnify the successful party while not unreasonably discouraging access to the court or unduly penalizing the losing party: McAllister at para 45; Barkwell 1 at para 57; VLM v Dominey Estate at para 9; AGS v RNS at para 35; Serinus Energy at para 23. Costs should be in an amount “that the losing party should reasonably be expected to pay to the winning party:” Barkwell 1 at para 59; Barkwell 2 at para 74; Kantor v Kantor at para 13. “[S]uccess is not a justification for disproportionate litigation:” VLM v Dominey Estate at para 9. [31] Proportionality can be understood to lie between (typically) the reasonable legal fees that should have been charged for the litigation steps and the percentage or portion of those reasonable fees payable by the unsuccessful party, taking into consideration the r 10.33 factors and other relevant factors, as those bear on the successful party, the unsuccessful party, and the litigation: Kantor v Kantor at para 13; McAllister at para 51; Serinus Energy at para 26. 2. Measures of Costs [32] The rules do not dictate a particular method of measuring proportional costs. In particular, a costs award need not be based on Schedule C. See rr 10.31(1), (3); McAllister at paras 25, 53, 54; Barkwell 1 at para 53; VLM v Dominey Estate at para 5. [33] The successful party's actual costs, assessed costs, reasonable solicitor-client costs, or Schedule C costs may serve as the basis for setting proportionate costs. See Grimes v UofL at para 49; Blaze Energy v Imperial Oil Resources, 2014 ABQB 509, Schutz J, as she then was, at para 61. [34] For the purposes of this decision, I need not offer a view on whether “Schedule C is not a mandated default method” for assessing costs: Barkwell 1 at para 53; Grimes v UofL at paras 28 and following; see AGS v RNS at para 43. 3. Solicitor and Own Client (Indemnity) Costs [35] Absent contractual or statutory obligations, setting costs at a successful party's actual costs, at the full indemnity or solicitor and own client costs level, is extremely rare. “[A]n award of solicitor and ‘own client’ costs is virtually unheard of except where provided by contract:” Luft v Taylor, Zinkhofer & Conway, 2017 ABCA 228 at para 78; Barkwell 1 at para 56; Kantor v Kantor at para 13; Vaillancourt v Carter at para 28; AGS v RNS at para 50; Serinus Energy at para 19. Solicitor and own client costs are the amounts the successful party's counsel can charge to the successful party as a matter of contract: Barkwell 1 at para 56. 4. Solicitor-Client Costs [36] Costs set at an indemnity (in the sense of 100% recovery) for an amount potentially less than actual fees is countenanced by the rules and the authorities. Solicitor-client costs, understood as reasonable or proportional solicitor-clients costs (not necessarily what was actually charged by the successful party's counsel) may be awarded. Solicitor-client costs “allow for the recovery of reasonable fees and disbursements for all steps reasonably necessary within the four corners of the litigation:” Vaillancourt v Carter at para 28. [37] These costs are typically awarded only in “rare and exceptional circumstances.” “As this Court has stated, solicitor-client costs are generally reserved for reprehensible, scandalous or outrageous conduct by a party and in rare and exceptional circumstances: Goldstick Estates (Re), 2019 ABCA 508 at para 24; Fech v Lewington, 2022 ABCA 154 at para 30:” Lay v Lay, 2024 ABCA 26 at para 17. See also Luft v Taylor, Zinkhofer & Conway at para 78; Vaillancourt v Carter at para 28; AGS v RNS at para 46; Serinus Energy at para 18; Gordon Estate (Re), 2024 ABCA 286 at para 21. (a) Circumstances Attracting Solicitor-Client Costs [38] In AGS v RNS at para 47, Justice Eamon confirmed the typical circumstances attracting solicitor-client costs (maintaining the citations referenced by Eamon J): [47] In Sidorsky [Sidorsky v CFCN Communications Limited, 1997 ABCA 280], the Court provided the following examples of rare cases when an award of reasonably incurred solicitor and client costs could be justified: [28] Costs are discretionary and as a general rule, a departure from party and party costs should only occur in rare and exceptional circumstances. Examples of such circumstances, outlined in Jackson v. Trimac Industries Ltd. (1993), 1993 CanLII 7031 (AB KB), 138 AR 161 at 172 (QB), include: 1. circumstances constituting blameworthiness in the conduct of the litigation by that party (Reese et al v Alberta (Minister of Forestry, Lands and Wildlife) et al, 1992 CanLII 2825 …, [1992] AJ No 745, 5 Alta LR (3d) 40 (QB)); 2. cases in which justice can only be done by a complete indemnification for costs (Foulis et al v Robinson; Gore Mutual Inc Co, Third Party, 1978 CanLII 1307…, [1978] OJ No 3596, 21 OR (2d) 769 (CA)); 3. where there is evidence that the plaintiff did something to hinder, delay or confuse the litigation, where there was no serious issue of fact or law which required these lengthy, expensive proceedings, where the positively misconducting party was “contemptuous” of the aggrieved party in forcing that aggrieved party to exhaust legal proceedings to obtain that which was obviously his (Max Sonnenberg Inc v Stewart, Smith (Canada) Ltd, 1986 CanLII 1771…, [1986] AJ No 1036, 48 Alta LR (2d) 367 (QB)); 4. an attempt to deceive the court and defeat justice, an attempt to delay, deceive and defeat justice, a requirement imposed on the plaintiff to prove facts that should have been admitted, thus prolonging the trial, unnecessary adjournments, concealing material documents from the plaintiffs and failing to produce material documents in a timely fashion (Olson v New Home Certification Program of Alberta, 1986 CanLII 1640 …, [1986] AJ No 347, 44 Alta LR (2d) 207 (QB)); 5. where the defendants were guilty of positive misconduct, where others should be deterred from like conduct and the defendants should be penalized beyond the ordinary order of costs (Dusik v Newton (1984), 51 BCLR 217, 1984 CanLII 690 …; 6. defendants found to be acting fraudulently and in breach of trust (Davis v Davis, 1981 CanLII 3545 …, [1981] MJ No 320, 9 Man R (2d) 236 (QB); 7. the defendants' fraudulent conduct in inducing a breach of contract and in presenting a deceptive statement of accounts to the court at trial (Kepic v Tecumseh Road Builder et al, [1987] OJ No 890, 23 OAC 72); 8. fraudulent conduct (Sturrock v Ancona Petroleums Ltd, 1990 CanLII 5563 …, [1990] AJ No 738, 111 AR 86 (QB)); and 9. an attempt to delay or hinder proceedings, an attempt to deceive or defeat justice, fraud or untrue or scandalous charges (Pharand Ski Corp v Alberta, 1991 CanLII 5931 …, [1991] AJ No 902, 83 Alta LR (2d) 152 (QB)). See also FIC Real Estate Fund v Phoenix Land Ventures, 2016 ABCA 303 at para 4; Prevatt v Prevatt at para 27. [39] While costs in estate litigation are being drawn into alignment with costs in other civil litigation contexts (see, e.g., Foote Estate (Re), 2010 ABQB 197, Graesser J at paras 16-19; Babchuk v Kutz, 2007 ABQB 81 and Petrowski v Petrowski Estate, 2009 ABQB 753, Moen J; Salter v Salter Estate, 2009 CanLII 28403, 50 ETR (3d) 227 (ONSC), Brown J, as he then was, at para 5), historically, courts in estate litigation cases countenanced solicitor-client costs payable from the estate not only for personal representative and successful parties, but unsuccessful parties: BA Schnurr and SB Tator, Estate Litigation, 2nd ed (Westlaw), § 19:2. (b) Not Pre-Litigation Conduct Alone [40] Justice Eamon followed the list of circumstances attracting solicitor-client costs in AGS v RNS with an important qualification, at para 48: [48] The Court must not base an award of solicitor-client costs on pre-litigation conduct alone, independent of other circumstances (Pillar Resource Services Inc v PrimeWest Energy Inc, 2017 ABCA 19 at para 1 - 10, 153, 158; Weatherford Canada Partnership v Artemis Kautschuk und Kunstoff-Technik GmbH, 2019 ABCA 92 at para 14; Breen v Foremost Industries Ltd, 2024 ABKB 9 at para 11-12, 22 and authorities cited therein). (c) Fiduciaries [41] A qualification to the no-pre-litigation-conduct qualification is that violations of duties by trustees or fiduciaries may attract solicitor-client costs. See Polar Ice Express Inc v Arctic Glacier Inc, 2009 ABCA 20 at para 21 (“[t]rusts or a fiduciary relationship might be an exception”); Evans v The Sports Corporation, 2011 ABQB 616, Graesser J at para 17, app dismissed 2013 ABCA 14; Lakusta Estate, 2010 ABQB 275, Hughes J, as she then was, at para 16; Bukkems Estate (Re), 2014 ABQB 678, Shelley J at para 10; Hrycyna v Hood, 2019 SKCA 30 at para 62; Siemens v Bawolin, 2002 SKCA 84 at paras 120-121. [42] However, a yet further refinement is that a proven breach of fiduciary duty does not in all cases attract solicitor-client costs. See Evans v The Sports Corporation at para 35(QB): “The Courts have not created any presumptions that breaches of trust or breaches of fiduciary duty should result in solicitor and client costs being awarded,” and para 58(QB). Breaches of fiduciary duty, like other violations of legal duties, occur across a spectrum of seriousness. Only breaches of fiduciary duty tending toward the more serious pole of the spectrum attract solicitor-client costs. See, e.g., HSBC Bank Canada v 1100336 Alberta Ltd. (Incredible Electronics Wholesale), 2012 ABQB 27, Marshall J at para 17; HSBC Bank Canada v Lourenco, 2012 ABQB 648, Goss J at paras 62-64, 66-67. I find the comments of Justice Mainella in Re Parkinson Estate, 2024 MBCA 52 at paras 117-120 to be illuminating: [117] My view is consistent with the historical context. Estate litigation has long drawn a distinction in costs awards between cases where the estate maladministration was due to inadvertence, lack of knowledge or poor judgment as compared to more egregious cases involving self-benefit, dishonesty or gross negligence (see Carmen S Thériault, ed, Widdifield on Executors and Trustees, 6th ed (Toronto: Thomson Reuters, 2024) (loose-leaf updated 2024, release 2) vol 1, ch 4 at 82.2-90 [Widdifield on Executors]). [118] Additionally, in situations involving a breach of a fiduciary duty outside of an estate context, reprehensible, scandalous or outrageous conduct by a fiduciary has been accepted to be an appropriate reason to consider pre-litigation conduct in awarding costs (see Winnipeg (City) v Sheegl, 2023 MBCA 63 at para 140; Hrycyna v Hood, 2019 SKCA 30 at para 67; Siemens v Bawolin, 2002 SKCA 84 at paras 120-21). The law should be harmonized in the same way in the context of estates. [119] I see no compelling legal reason to require a court to overlook what may be important context in fashioning a costs award where a fiduciary has come up far short in meeting the stringent obligations the law expects. As Dubin JA (as he then was) explained in Foulis v Robinson, 1978 CarswellOnt 466 at para 20, 1978 CanLII 1307 (ONCA), there are cases “in which justice can only be done by a complete indemnification for costs”. In the right set of circumstances, an award of solicitor and client costs based on a trustee's pre-litigation conduct is entirely in keeping with the court's supervisory role to ensure that estates are not unwarrantedly depleted and to guarantee the integrity of fiduciary relationships. [120] The respondent's reliance on the Court's comments in Dalrymple v DeMeyer Estate, 2022 MBQB 31 at para 31 [Dalrymple], is not persuasive as that case is distinguishable. In Dalrymple, the Court found that the executors' conduct did not meet the high threshold of reprehensible, scandalous or outrageous conduct. The Court did not in any way suggest that if the executors' conduct had met that high threshold, that would not be a factor that could be considered in fixing costs pursuant to r 57.01 of the KB Rules. 5. Enhanced Costs and Percentage of Solicitor-Client Costs [43] A practical problem is that between cases warranting indemnity through reasonable solicitor-client costs and cases whose costs can be settled by reference to the Schedule C tariff without alteration lies a broad range of cases involving many differing factors relevant to costs. The principle of proportionality would suggest that indemnification beyond the Schedule C tariff may be appropriate for some of these cases. How are proportional costs to be secured? (a) Enhanced Schedule C Costs [44] If the facially applicable tariff is inadequate in the litigation and pre-litigation (if applicable) circumstances, one method of achieving proportional costs is through awarding “enhanced costs” by modifying Schedule C costs: see Serinus Energy at para 16. Rules 10.31(1) and (3) and the authorities expressly authorize an array of tools or mechanisms for arriving at a reasonable costs award. Justice Shelley wrote in Weatherford Canada Partnership v Addie, 2018 ABQB 571, affd 2019 ABCA 92 at para 55 (QB) that “Alberta courts have recognized that when Schedule C fees are inadequate, courts may use several different methods for determining appropriate costs, including the application of multipliers to a column, extra lump sums, or some fraction of solicitor-client costs ….” See also Ed Miller Sales & Rentals Ltd v Caterpillar Tractor Co, 1998 ABCA 118 at para 4. (b) Percentage of Solicitor-Client Costs [45] Another method of measuring proportional costs is through an award of costs representing a percentage of reasonable solicitor-client costs. This costs measure has a long history in Alberta civil litigation but was revisited in McAllister. [46] The Court of Appeal has confirmed that in this costs context, as in the context of full recovery of solicitor-client costs, the costs at issue are solicitor-client costs, not costs set by the successful party's contractual obligation to pay its counsel's account, not the quantum of fees charged by counsel and paid by the successful party: Barkwell 1 at paras 55, 56. Rather, the multiplicand solicitor and client costs are the amounts that might reasonably be paid for the successful party's legal services: Barkwell 1 at para 56; Kantor v Kantor at para 13 (taking into account the factors in r 10.2); AGS v RNS at para 36. Further, the percentage of fees to be paid cannot be disproportionate to, e.g., the issues and amounts of the litigation: Barkwell 1 at para 57; VLM v Dominey Estate at para 8. “The issue is not simply how much the successful party spent, but how much that party can reasonably expect the other party to pay …. The costs awarded must be proportionate to the amounts in issue:” Barkwell 2 at para 74; VLM v Dominey Estate at para 8 (“The issue is … what amount the unsuccessful party can fairly be expected to contribute”); AGS v RNS at para 37; Sutherland v Sutherland, 2023 ABCA 185 at para 4. [47] In contrast to the full recovery of solicitor-client costs cases, the guideline or general level of partial indemnity is in the 40 - 50% range, keeping in mind that indemnification may be greater or lesser than this guideline: McAllister at paras 41-51. [48] One might say that our Courts have recognized implicitly and in practice an indemnity subprinciple, falling under the broader principle of proportionality. See the Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, RRO 1990, Reg 194, r 57.01(1) (0.a): 57.01 (1) In exercising its discretion under section 131 of the Courts of Justice Act to award costs, the court may consider, in addition to the result in the proceeding and any offer to settle or to contribute made in writing, (0.a) the principle of indemnity, including, where applicable, the experience of the lawyer for the party entitled to the costs as well as the rates charged and the hours spent by that lawyer …. (i) Circumstances Attracting Percentage of Solicitor-Client Costs [49] Costs set at a percentage indemnity of reasonable solicitor-client costs do not require proof of the typical factors supporting full indemnity of reasonable solicitor-client costs: McAllister at para 50 (were those factors established, a successful party would doubtless prefer full to partial indemnity). [50] In what circumstances may costs be set at a percentage of reasonable solicitor-client costs? I refer to GO Community Centre at paras 148-150: [148] Historically, the percentage indemnity approach has been associated with lengthy, complicated litigation: Ed Miller at para 7 (“The suit was extraordinarily long …. And it is believed to have been the longest completed civil trial in Alberta history”) and para 12 (“Another factor is the seriousness of the suit. The amounts were enormous, the charges were grave, and the business implications considerable. If ever there was a suit which did not call for penny-pinching half measures by the defendant, this was it”) …. [149] The percentage indemnity approach has more recently been applied in less lengthy but nevertheless (to my eye) complex or at least moderately complex litigation, cases found perhaps part-way on the continuum between “the common stream of cases” and Ed Miller-style trials: Styles [Styles v Caravan Trailer Lodges of Alberta Limited, 2019 ABQB 558, Jones J]; Remington [Remington v Crystal Creek Homes Inc, 2018 ABQB 644, Jones J]; Athabasca Minerals [Athabasca Minerals Inc v Syncrude Canada Ltd, 2018 ABQB 551, Jones J] (five days allocated to reading time: at para 28); Estate of Montgomery, 2019 ABQB 833, DB Nixon J [as he then was]; Intact Insurance [Intact Insurance Company v Clauson Cold & Cooler Ltd, 2019 ABQB 225, Dilts J] at paras 17-20; see Orbis Engineering [Orbis Engineering Field Services v Taifa Engineering Ltd, 2019 ABQB 592, Mah J] at para 12. [150] An important feature of the cases to which the percentage indemnity approach has been extended is that the parties were sophisticated and similarly situated economically. One does not hold surplus power. There is not a “significant imbalance in the power and means of the parties;” “the playing field is level:” Styles at para 59; see Remington at paras 31, 33-35, 42. Both, then, can be expected to face similar types of legal accounts. Both are proceeding with knowledge of what the litigation is costing: Remington at para 29; Athabasca Minerals at para 65; Blough v Busy Music Inc, 2020 ABQB 19, Jones J at para 29. Justice Jones commented in Remington at para 34 that “applying a percentage of fees incurred approach seems to me to respect their right to choose how much they are willing to spend to make their point.” See also JBRO Holdings Inc v Dynasty Power Inc, 2022 ABCA 258 at para 25; Serinus Energy at para 55. [51] On this last point, again one might suggest that a subprinciple concerning the parties' “reasonable expectations” is at work, as in Ontario r 57.01(1)(0.b), “the amount of costs that an unsuccessful party could reasonably expect to pay in relation to the step in the proceeding for which costs are being fixed.” [emphasis added] See Barkwell 1 at para 59: [59] Further, if the trial judge decides to make a costs award based on a percentage of solicitor and client costs the analysis must go further. The question is not just whether the solicitor and client costs are reasonable as between solicitor and client, but whether the quantum represents an amount that the losing party in the litigation should reasonably be expected to pay to the winning party …. [emphasis added] [52] McAllister itself concerned an almost completed piece of protracted litigation, which included a trial, and the many steps required to bring the matter to trial and involved “arguably novel liability” (paras 1, 64). (ii) Setting Costs at a Percentage of Solicitor-Client Costs [53] “[T]here is no presumption in the Rules that the successful party is entitled to any particular level of indemnification:” VLM v Dominey Estate at para 6. A successful party seeking percentage indemnity costs must show that this is the appropriate measure of costs. [54] The Court of Appeal stated in Barkwell 1 at para 60 that [60] If the winning party seeks a costs award based on a percentage of solicitor and client fees, that request must be justified by a consideration of the factors in r 10.2 that are relevant to the reasonableness of a fee. That includes the importance of the issues, the circumstances of the client, the manner in which the services were provided, the skill and responsibility involved, and other relevant considerations. Many of those same issues are also listed in r 10.33, which in addition to the amount in issue, refers to the complexity of the action and the conduct of the parties. Also relevant are things like the hourly rates being charged (including paralegal or administrative time), whether those rates were appropriate given the seniority and experience of counsel, whether the work was being done by lawyers of appropriate seniority, the number of counsel involved, whether the duration and intensity of pre-trial questioning was appropriate or excessive or disproportionate, whether unnecessary interlocutory proceedings were launched and the outcome of those proceedings, and whether the ultimate fee was proportionate to the issues. See also McAllister at para 46; Ho v Lau, 2023 ABKB 15, Lema J at para 42. 6. Schedule C Costs [55] Costs are often awarded by reference to Schedule C to the rules. “Using Schedule C has the advantage of providing parties with greater certainty as to their exposure to costs, it is simple, efficient, and inexpensive to apply, and in many cases avoids the need for lengthy inquiries into and assessment of the appropriate level of costs: McAllister at paras 59-60, 62:” Barkwell 1 at para 53: VLM v Dominey Estate at para 5; AGS v RNS at para 38. In many cases Schedule C represents an appropriate level of indemnification: VLM v Dominey Estate at para 6. [56] Schedule C to the rules provides a rough measure of proportional costs, presupposing notional reasonable legal fees (the costs that should reasonably have been incurred given the issues), using the amount of claims as a proxy for more granular r 10.33 considerations, and setting specific amounts that are in effect 40-50% of the notional reasonable legal fees: see McAllister at para 37; Barkwell 1 at paras 57, 58; VLM v Dominey Estate at para 6; Serinus Energy at para 26. Schedule C costs may be refined by consideration of the r 10.33 factors (r 10.31(3)(b)). [57] As indicated, Schedule C costs may be “enhanced” by various techniques to bring a costs award into line with proportional costs. See also Justice Renke's summary of the law of costs in Garbera Estate, 2024 ABKB 641 at paragraphs 18-48. Another useful summary is found in Justice Marion's decisions in Serinus Energy PLC v. SysGen Solutions Group Ltd., 2024 ABKB 123 at paragraphs 10-27, and Savoie v. Lambert, 2024 ABKB 744 at paragraphs 10-33. In Champagne v. Sidorsky, 2018 ABCA 394, 2018 CarswellAlta 2795, 78 Alta. L.R. (6th) 1, 28 C.P.C. (8th) 251, the Court discussed three specific principles of the law of costs (costs for the successful party; wasted costs; and partial indemnity): [21] This costs application required the assimilation of three overlapping principles underlying the law of costs. The first principle is that the successful party is presumptively entitled to costs, and that those costs are payable forthwith: R. 10.29(1). Special reasons are generally required to deny a successful party its costs, and very unusual reasons are required to justify having the successful party actually pay costs: Kretschmer v Terrigno, 2012 ABCA 345 (CanLII) at paras. 1, 116, 539 AR 212, 77 Alta LR (5th) 300. [22] The second principle is that a party can be denied “wasted” costs, such as costs which arise from that party's own carelessness, misconduct or default: R. 10.33(2). This situation can apply when a party applies to withdraw an admission that was improvidently made, to open up a noting in default, to amend defective pleadings, or where it must apply to repeat a procedural step because of self-generated deficiencies: see David M. Gottlieb Professional Corp. v Nahal, 2013 ABCA 154 (CanLII) at para. 7, 544 AR 339, 89 Alta LR (5th) 351. A particular manifestation of this principle is found in R. 3.66: 3.66 (1) Subject to subrule (2), the costs, if any, as a result of an amendment to a pleading are to be borne by the party filing the amendment unless (a) the amendment is a response to an amended pleading, or (b) the Court otherwise orders. (2) The costs of a contested application to amend a pleading are in the discretion of the Court, in accordance with rule 10.29 [General rule for payment of litigation costs]. While this rule creates a presumption that the amending party must bear the costs of the amendment, it is not absolute. The judge's wide discretion over costs is maintained both in R. 3.66(1)(b) with respect to amendments generally, and R. 3.66(2) with respect to contested amendments. [23] The third principle is that costs should not provide a complete indemnity. This is to ensure that parties only take procedural steps that are proportionate to the issues involved, the possible remedies, and any prejudice that may result. If parties were entitled to indemnity costs every time they were successful, there would be an incentive towards “scorched earth” litigation. Any time an applicant sought relief that resulted in whole or in part from its own default, the respondent might be tempted to fight to the end, even though the moving party could meet the test for the requested relief. R. 3.66(2) reflects this principle, because it identifies as a special category contested amendment applications. If a party applies to amend pleadings, and it seems that the amendment will likely be permitted, the respondent is not entitled to resist the amendment on the expectation that it will nevertheless receive costs under R. 3.66(1). In Boardwalk REIT Properties Holding Ltd. v. Condominium Corp. No. 0822896, 2019 ABQB 260, 2019 CarswellAlta 678, Justice Dunlop said: [6] Rule 10.29 addresses entitlement to costs; it is irrelevant to the scale of costs. In GO Community Centre v. Clark Builders and Stantec Consulting Ltd, 2020 ABQB 203, 2020 CarswellAlta 548, Justice Renke set out the “purpose” of awarding costs: [59] The purposes of the costs regime can be enumerated in different ways, but costs serve two direct purposes and one higher order purpose (which in turn serves further purposes promoting the rule of law). First, costs provide some compensation to a successful litigant. The litigant is not required to shoulder alone all of the expense of legal vindication. In that way, costs serve the higher order objective of enhancing access to justice by providing deferred reimbursement to a successful litigant. This higher-order objective also imposes constraints on costs, which I'll return to below. Second, costs promote rational and litigation norm-consistent decision making. On the one hand, costs discourage frivolous claims and discourage improper litigation behaviour. On the other hand, by adding a measure of predictable risk to litigation, costs can contribute to incentives for settlement. These objectives promote access to justice by freeing the litigation system from cases that need not or should not be litigated. See, e.g., Geophysical Service Incorporated v Falkland Oil and Gas Ltd, 2019 ABQB 314, Woolley J at paras 16 and 28 and McAllister v Calgary (City), 2018 ABQB 999, Kubik J at para 14: [14] Schedule C costs serve many useful purposes in litigation. First, they reward a successful party by compensating them for the significant steps taken in the litigation. Second, they allow the parties to effectively measure the risk of costs associated with the litigation. Further, the parties often make arguments on points that the court does not have to deal with, because of the way the decision unfolds. The general rule contemplates that the party who achieves substantial success on the appeal will receive costs, even if that party is not totally successful, nor successful on every issue or argument. Jaycock (2001), 295 A.R. 276 (Q.B.), an unsuccessful plaintiff asked he be given time to pay the costs awarded. Veit, J. agreed that she had jurisdiction to do so, but declined to do so. At pp. 279–281, Her Ladyship said: Although there is no specific provision which allows the court to grant time to pay costs, I accept that such time to pay may be allowed under the court's general discretion in the matter of costs. I have caused a cursory examination to be made of the Rules of Practice of certain other Canadian jurisdictions to determine whether there might be any jurisdiction which has addressed this issue in its Rules. I have been unable to find any such reference. In the absence of any statement in the Rules concerning the exercise of the court's jurisdiction in the matter of costs, I have concluded that it would not be appropriate for the court to exercise its discretion to allow costs to be paid over time. This does not, of course, prevent the parties from reaching an agreement on this issue; indeed, the lawyer for the defendants indicated at the costs hearing that he would seriously present any reasonable proposal for paying costs over time to his clients. In reaching the conclusion that courts should not give litigants time to pay court costs, I have relied on first principles and on analogy to other areas of civil practice. The first factor to take into account in this analysis is that the impecuniosity, or lack of financial resources of a litigant, is no reason to shield that litigant from the full effect of costs. Impecuniosity will mean, of course, that the party who has obtained the costs award, like a party who obtains a judgment, may not be able to recover the full amount of the award. But the making of the award constitutes at least a moral victory for the person who obtains the benefit of the award, even if the award can never be enforced. The second factor is that costs focus backwards, that is they relate to fees and expenditures which have already been paid or incurred. Therefore, the person who is awarded costs is, as a matter of principle, entitled to the payment of those costs as soon as they are ordered. There was a period during which this statement of principle would not have applied in Alberta to interlocutory matters; however, since Alberta has moved to a “pay as you go” basis for the payment of costs even on interlocutory matters, such costs are payable as soon as they as ordered. This is particularly true, of course, in situations such as this one where the costs award is linked to a final decision in proceedings … The third factor to consider is the public policy which supports the making of final decisions in the court system. This applies even to situations in which a substantive award is made, for example to a victim of a motor vehicle accident; that award may cover both damages or payments that have been made in the past as well as damages that may arise in the future. A negligent driver is not entitled to make periodic payments to a successful plaintiff; the driver who has been found negligent has a legal obligation to pay the whole of the judgment immediately. … Even stronger policy considerations apply to costs awards: there is no comparable risk of over-compensation in costs awards because only past events influence the making of the award. In this context, it is important to note that the relatively recent increases in Alberta's Schedule C tariff of costs recognize the reality of the high costs of the litigation process. It costs litigants a lot of money to initiate, or defend, civil litigation; when a litigant is successful, it is only fair that the litigant should be re-imbursed in a timely way for some portion of those costs. The last factor to be taken into account in determining whether the court should establish a schedule of payment for costs is the purpose of awarding costs: costs constitute the basis of discipline in the civil court process. Delaying the payment of costs might tend to undermine the principle that costs which are paid when incurred keep the litigants in touch with the financial reality of litigation; this reality check should promote and nurture reasonable settlements. It is true, of course, that in criminal proceedings, a convict may be given time to pay a fine and that time may be extended from time to time. However, the practice in criminal proceedings is not comparable to the practice in civil proceedings because, in criminal matters, the ability of an offender to pay a fine is a matter which is relevant to the imposition of the penalty. As indicated above, the impecuniosity of a litigant is not relevant to the issue of costs in a civil proceeding. Moreover, it is important to notice that a fine is a form of retribution to the community at large; a convict who cannot afford to pay a fine can, instead, work off the fine by doing community service work. In civil proceedings, an award of costs is not a punishment and is not imposed for the benefit of the community; it is a re-payment to a litigant of what have been found to be unnecessary expenses incurred for the purpose of the lawsuit. In summary, therefore, there are many reasons of principle why a court should not deprive a litigant of the full and timely benefit of costs which have been awarded. 9. Payment forthwith In Snihur v. In this situation the courts have devised two alternatives known respectively as a Bullock order and a Sanderson order. See also Craven v Chmura, 2015 ONSC 4843 at para 9. 28 Erb J took a similar approach in Archer v St John, 2008 ABQB 245 at para 26, where she said the following: There is no evidence before me that the Defendant, Laureen St. John, is impecunious. Nevertheless, a balancing of equities leads me to conclude that any risk of non-recovery of costs from Ms. St. John should be borne by the Plaintiff, Devon Archer, rather than Mountain View Credit Union and the Estate of Gerald Archer. [Emphasis added]. 29 In Archer, Erb J referred to the “risk of non-recovery,” which requires the plaintiff to undertake a risk assessment when commencing and conducting litigation. In Rowe v Investors Syndicate Ltd (1984), 46 CPC 209 at 271 (Ont H Ct Jus), Henry J explained this risk assessment as follows: The equitable issue is whether the plaintiffs or [the successful defendant] should bear the risk of non-recovery. A “Bullock” order will prejudice the plaintiffs, a “Sanderson” order the successful defendant. As between the two equity lies with the [successful] defendant. The plaintiffs took the risk of bringing [the successful defendant] to Court and did not succeed. See also SGH v Gorsline, 2001 ABQB 671 at para 21. 30 Because Valour Park is impecunious, a Sanderson order places the risk of non-recovery on the successful defendants. The Plaintiffs, in the case at bar, took the risk that they might not be able to recover costs from Valour Park because of Valour Park's impecuniosity. Although this Court does not see this as “the determining factor,” it is one factor that this Court must consider in weighing the balance. See also Rowe at 214. 20. Costs in the Cause when Trial Does Not Occur The defendants say that because there was no trial, no costs for pre-trial procedures where costs were reserved for disposition by the trial judge can be awarded. I disagree. It was clearly the intention of the judges who decided the interlocutory motions that costs would be dealt with. They did not say that there would be no costs for those procedures, or that there would be no costs in the event of settlement. In the event, because there was a settlement, there was no trial of the substantive issues in the lawsuit. However, the decision about who is to get what costs remains an issue to be determined. It is appropriate that the judge who had been assigned to hear the trial should determine costs. Lines v. Brink (1994), 24 Alta. L.R. (3d) 227 (Q.B.), at 234, per Veit J. 21. Costs on Appeal This is a special application, after the oral hearing, for an award of costs to the successful appellant for the original hearing in Queen's Bench. These were not awarded at the oral hearing because no mention was made of them at that time. Apparently, counsel assumed that our practice is that an award of costs to the successful appellant automatically includes a reversal of a costs award at trial. It does not. Our practice is, as the Practice Note of November 15, 1991 says, that costs of the appeal follow the event unless some special circumstances come to our attention. Costs of trial must, on the other hand, be sought in the factum and at the oral hearing, or the court might refuse to award them on that ground alone. We treat the present application as, first, leave to reargue the costs issue, and make a request for trial costs. We would grant the leave because of the mistake, and because no harm came from it other than the need, and nuisance, for this application. We are not likely to take that view in the future, now that this case removes any doubt about our practice. West Edmonton Mall Ltd. v. McDonald's Restaurants of Canada Ltd. (1993), 145 A.R. 76 (C.A.), at 77, per the court. The Practice Note referred to by the Court of Appeal is Court of Appeal Practice Note H—Costs in Civil Matters, and is reproduced in App. IV, infra. In Hogarth v. Rocky Mountain Slate Inc., 2013 ABCA 116, 2013 CarswellAlta 835, 87 Alta. L.R. (5th) 108, the Court said, in relation to costs awards made at appeal, at paragraph 12: 12 On appeal, the appellant Simonson was successful in having the entire judgment against him set aside. As such, he is entitled to assessed costs of the appeal. The respondents argue that Simonson should not receive full, or any costs, because he was not successful on all of the arguments that he raised. Costs, however, are not usually allocated on an issue by issue basis: Mahe v. Boulianne, 2010 ABCA 74, at para. 6, 21 Alta LR (5th) 277. It is rare for a litigant to be successful on each and every issue, but that does not mean that litigants should not argue every issue reasonably raised on the record, nor does that disentitle them to costs. At the end of the day Simonson was successful on appeal in having the entire judgment set aside, and he is entitled to costs. 22. Successful Appeal Usually Overrides Costs Awarded at Trial In Ed Miller Sales & Rentals Ltd. v. Caterpillar Tractor Co., [1996] 9 W.W.R. 449 (Alta. C.A.), this Court held that where the appellant succeeded entirely on appeal, there was no longer any basis for the award of costs at trial. . . . . . The general rule is that costs are awarded throughout to the successful party on appeal. Nonetheless, the Court may choose not to disturb an award of costs at trial in favour of a losing party in a case involving special and peculiar problems, where, for example, an act of the state has compelled a response to protect preceived rights concerning a constitutional matter of fundamental importance. Public School Boards' Assn. (Alberta) v. Alberta (Attorney General) (1998), 64 Alta. L.R. (3d) 390 (C.A.), at 395–96, per curiam, [additional reasons to (1998), 60 Alta. L.R. (3d) 62 C.A.; leave to appeal allowed (1998), 235 N.R. 395n S.C.C.; leave to appeal refused (1999), 237 A.R. 200n (S.C.C.)]. 23. Appeals from Applications Judge In 1808882 Alberta Ltd. v. Moderno Ventures Ltd., 2018 ABQB 1000, 2018 CarswellAlta 2993, Justice Eamon noted that while a party appealing an order granted by a Master was allowed to produce evidence not put before the Master, there can be costs consequences if it is found that the late production of the evidence resulted in a waste of time. His Lordship said: [12] I also take into account the Appellant's conduct of the summary judgment proceedings. Appeals from Masters' decisions are de novo and a party is permitted to add evidence and arguments on appeal. That does not mean there are no costs consequences for failing to efficiently conduct the proceedings. As I said in my appeal reasons, [71]… Where decisive additional evidence or a new argument is adduced on appeal, any prejudice can be addressed by penalizing the successful appellant in costs for wasting the application before the Master where appropriate. Of course, other considerations might also factor into that decision such as litigation misconduct by the other side, time pressures in the proceeding below such as those often seen in assembling evidence or responding in the context of a morning chambers list, or the like. [13] I agree with Master Prowse QC that the Plaintiff 180's evidence on the application in Master's Chambers was wholly inadequate. Also, the Plaintiff 180 wanted to cross-examine on the Defendant's affidavit, but was unable to arrange it and made a strategic decision to proceed in Master's Chambers without it (Transcript, May 2, 2018, pp 30–31). On appeal, the Appellant conducted the cross-examination which it earlier decided to forego and added substantial new evidence to the appeal record including that testimony. [14] The Appellant's approach to summary judgment was akin to litigation by instalment, starting from an obviously weak position before the learned Master and curing the gaps on appeal. That conduct unreasonably and unnecessarily delayed the litigation and increased cost and effort. Although the Appellant has already borne adverse costs consequences for its failure in the initial application, its costs award on the appeal should be reduced to address the prejudice of delay and wasted effort associated with its approach and encourage parties to reasonably prepare summary judgment applications by placing the necessary record before the Master. The same approach was taken by Justice Hollins in Prestige Granite & Marble Inc. v. Maillot Homes Inc., 2018 ABQB 1040: [23] On that point, I am in agreement with the approach of my brother, Justice Eamon, who in a recent case in which an appellant relied on new evidence not presented to the Master, deprived the appellant of part of its costs, notwithstanding its success on appeal; 1808882 Alberta Ltd v Moderno Ventures Ltd. 2018 ABQB 1000 (CanLII). Justice Mah, in Alberta Finance & Mortgage Corp. v Bruce Steel Erectors Ltd., 2018 ABQB 907 (CanLII) has done likewise. Rule 10.33(2) provides a menu of considerations for this Court on costs, including steps taken which have unnecessarily delayed the action. In this case, while the Plaintiff successfully appealed the Master's Order, all that has really happened is that the parties have now exchanged the evidence necessary to allow them to resolve matters or properly prepare for trial. See also: Rudichuk v. Genesis Land Development Corp., 2019 ABQB 133, 2019 CarswellAlta 339 at paragraph 56. 24. Costs on Third Party Proceedings In Condominium Corporation 052 0580 (o/a The Tradition at Southbrook) v. Carrington Holdings Ltd., 2024 ABKB 55, Justice Mandziuk referred to a situation in which an unsuccessful plaintiff should pay the costs of a third party: [33] The Plaintiff's action was dismissed in the Delay Application. The Plaintiff did not directly sue the Third Parties, but they were brought in because of the Plaintiff's claim. They incurred costs as a result. The Third Parties faced liability, and they took steps in response to the Plaintiff's action which has now been dismissed. [34] Weatherall v Seaba, 2009 ABQB 173 sets out situations where the Plaintiff should, in fairness, pay the costs of third parties. One such situation is “where the third party proceedings follow naturally and inevitably upon the institution of the Plaintiff's action, in the sense that the defendant had no real alternative but to join the third party” (at para 16). [35] The work of a developer is undertaken by an array of contracted parties. Here, the Plaintiff sued the developer, and it flows naturally that the developer would have joined the myriad of sub-contractors which the Third Parties comprise. I am satisfied that the Defendant's decision to bring the Third Parties into this action was inevitable upon the initiation of the action by the Plaintiffs. 25. When Does The Rule Apply? In Chernetz v. Eagle Copters Ltd. (2003), 24 Alta. L.R. (4th) 297 (Q.B.), McMahon J., at p. 300, noted that “[t]he rule does not define ‘unsuccessful’.” After discussing whether “substantial success” was sufficient to engage the rule, his Lordship concluded, at p. 300, that: In respect of the production of documents and claims to privilege, it is my view that the substantial success test is not adequate. It is not enough to be mostly or substantially correct to win costs. … To put it briefly, he who claims privilege had best be right if he wishes costs.

sentences.text: Commentary § 10.29:1 Rule 10.29 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta.
Reg.
General rule In Weatherford Canada Partnership v.

Artemis Kautschuk and Kunstoff-Technik GmbH, 2019 ABCA 92, 2019 CarswellAlta 422, the Court said: [11] The discretion to award costs must be exercised judicially and in line with the factors in r 10.33: Stewart Estate v TAQA North Limited, 2016 ABCA 144 (CanLII) at para 26, 35 Alta LR

The general rule is that costs are awarded on a party and party basis, and that this should represent partial indemnification of the successful party—approximately 40–50% of actual costs: Trizec Equities Ltd v Ellis-Don Management Services Ltd, 1999 ABQB 801 (CanLII) at para 20–21, 251 AR 101
Blaze Energy Ltd v Imperial Oil Resources, 2014 ABQB 509 (CanLII) at para 68, [2014] AJ No 916 (QL).

[12] Party and party costs balance two competing interests: the unfairness of requiring a successful party whose conduct is not blameworthy to bear any costs and the chilling effect on parties bringing or defending claims if the unsuccessful party is required to bear all the costs: LSI Logic Corporation of Canada, Inc v Logani, 2001 ABQB 968 (CanLII) at para 5, [2002] 4 WWR 531 (LSI Logic).
The result of this balance is the concept of partial indemnification through party and party costs to the successful party.

[13] While costs are always in the discretion of the court, the cases recognize that when the litigation is complex and the amount at stake in the action in dispute greatly exceeds column 5, courts may award a multiplier of column 5 to help achieve the level of indemnification appropriate for party and party costs: Rocky Mountain House at para 13.
To do so is not an error in principle.
[14] An award of solicitor and client costs will be rare and must be based on a finding of intentional misconduct during the litigation.
LSI Logic at paras 5–6; Luft v Taylor, Zinkhofer & Conway, 2017 ABCA 228 (CanLII) at para 75, 53 Alta LR (6d) 44 (Luft).
Solicitor and client costs indemnify for costs that arise within the four corners of the litigation.
Full indemnification costs, also known as solicitor and own client costs, compensate for services that are not strictly essential to the litigation.
LSI Logic at para 4; Luft at para 77.
They are “virtually unheard of” except when provided for by contract: Luft at para 78.
Paragraph 14 of Weatherford was quoted with approval in Lotoski v.
Lotoski, 2019 ABCA 262, 2019 CarswellAlta 1267 (at paragraph 3).
In Norris v.

Norris, 2024 ABKB 600, Justice Renke gave this summary of the law relating to the awarding of costs: [25] The Court of Appeal has recently provided guidance respecting costs determinations in cases including McAllister v Calgary (City), 2021 ABCA 25
Barkwell v McDonald, 2023 ABCA 87 (Barkwell 1)
Barkwell v McDonald, 2023 ABCA 183 (Barkwell 2)
Sunridge Nissan v McRuer, 2023 ABCA 128 at para 57
Petroupoulos v Petropoulos, 2023 ABCA 193, Pentelechuk JA
Kantor v Kantor, 2023 ABCA 329
VLM v Dominey Estate, 2023 ABCA 382; and Vaillancourt v Carter, 2024 ABCA 65.
For background discussions, see (e.g.) GO Community Centre v Clark Builders and Stantec Consulting Ltd, 2020 ABQB 203 at paras 56-163
Ehli v Lamanator Coatings Ltd, 2024 ABKB 339
Grimes v Governors of the University of Lethbridge, 2023 ABKB 432, Graesser J, passim
Serinus Energy PLC v SysGen Solutions Group Ltd, 2024 ABKB 123, Marion J at paras 10-27
AGS v RNS, 2024 ABKB 280, Eamon J at paras 24-50
Prevatt v Prevatt, 2024 ABKB 386, DJ Reed J at paras 13-26.
[26] Under r 10.29(1), a successful party is generally entitled to a costs award: McAllister at para 21; Serinus Energy at para 11.
This is to say that the unsuccessful party is generally obligated to pay costs to the successful party.
[27] Generally again, on the Alberta approach to costs, the unsuccessful party is not obligated to pay the full legal fees actually incurred by the successful party: McAllister at paras 37, 41
Barkwell 1 at para 58
VLM v Dominey Estate at para 4
AGS v RNS at para 30
Serinus Energy at para 24
RVB Managements Ltd v Rocky Mountain House (Town), 2015 ABCA 304 at para 14
Trizec Equities Limited v Ellis-Don Management Services Ltd, 1999 ABQB 801, Mason J at para 21.
[28] The costs determination is “discretionary,” but not unfettered.
The discretion must be exercised judicially.
The discretion remains governed by principle, the rules and authorities: Styles v Caravan Trailer Lodges of Alberta Limited, 2019 ABQB 558, Jones J at para 47
Grimes v UofL at para 51
Stewart Estate v TAQA North Ltd, 2017 ABCA 144 at para 26
Vaillancourt v Carter at para 24
Serinus Energy at para 10.
[29] But how is the amount of costs to be gauged?

Proportionality [30] The overarching principle is proportionality: Barkwell 1 at para 57; VLM v Dominey Estate at para 9; Petropoulos at para 18; Serinus Energy at para 27; Goldstick Estates (Re), 2019 ABCA 508 at para 31.
Costs should reasonably indemnify the successful party while not unreasonably discouraging access to the court or unduly penalizing the losing party: McAllister at para 45
Barkwell 1 at para 57
VLM v Dominey Estate at para 9
AGS v RNS at para 35
Serinus Energy at para 23.
Costs should be in an amount “that the losing party should reasonably be expected to pay to the winning party:” Barkwell 1 at para 59
Barkwell 2 at para 74
Kantor v Kantor at para 13. “[S]uccess is not a justification for disproportionate litigation:” VLM v Dominey Estate at para 9.
[31] Proportionality can be understood to lie between

(typically) the reasonable legal fees that should have been charged for the litigation steps and the percentage or portion of those reasonable fees payable by the unsuccessful party, taking into consideration the r 10.33 factors and other relevant factors, as those bear on the successful party, the unsuccessful party, and the litigation: Kantor v Kantor at para 13
McAllister at para 51
Serinus Energy at para 26.
Measures of Costs [32] The rules do not dictate a particular method of measuring proportional costs.
In particular, a costs award need not be based on Schedule C.
See rr 10.31(1), (3); McAllister at paras 25, 53, 54; Barkwell 1 at para 53; VLM v Dominey Estate at para 5.
[33] The successful party's actual costs, assessed costs, reasonable solicitor-client costs, or Schedule C costs may serve as the basis for setting proportionate costs.
See Grimes v UofL at para 49; Blaze Energy v Imperial Oil Resources, 2014 ABQB 509, Schutz J, as she then was, at para 61.

[34] For the purposes of this decision, I need not offer a view on whether “Schedule C is not a mandated default method” for assessing costs: Barkwell 1 at para 53; Grimes v UofL at paras 28 and following; see AGS v RNS at para 43.

Solicitor and Own Client (Indemnity) Costs [35] Absent contractual or statutory obligations, setting costs at a successful party's actual costs, at the full indemnity or solicitor and own client costs level, is extremely rare. “[A]n award of solicitor and ‘own client’ costs is virtually unheard of except where provided by contract:” Luft v Taylor, Zinkhofer & Conway, 2017 ABCA 228 at para 78
Barkwell 1 at para 56
Kantor v Kantor at para 13
Vaillancourt v Carter at para 28
AGS v RNS at para 50
Serinus Energy at para 19.
Solicitor and own client costs are the amounts the successful party's counsel can charge to the successful party as a matter of contract: Barkwell 1 at para 56.
Solicitor-Client Costs [36] Costs set at an indemnity (in the sense of 100% recovery) for an amount potentially less than actual fees is countenanced by the rules and the authorities.
Solicitor-client costs, understood as reasonable or proportional solicitor-clients costs (not necessarily what was actually charged by the successful party's counsel) may be awarded.
Solicitor-client costs “allow for the recovery of reasonable fees and disbursements for all steps reasonably necessary within the four corners of the litigation:” Vaillancourt v Carter at para 28.

[37] These costs are typically awarded only in “rare and exceptional circumstances.” “As this Court has stated, solicitor-client costs are generally reserved for reprehensible, scandalous or outrageous conduct by a party and in rare and exceptional circumstances: Goldstick Estates (Re), 2019 ABCA 508 at para 24
Fech v Lewington, 2022 ABCA 154 at para 30:” Lay v Lay, 2024 ABCA 26 at para 17.
See also Luft v Taylor, Zinkhofer & Conway at para 78; Vaillancourt v Carter at para 28; AGS v RNS at para 46; Serinus Energy at para 18; Gordon Estate (Re), 2024 ABCA 286 at para 21.

(a) Circumstances Attracting Solicitor-Client Costs [38] In AGS v RNS at para 47, Justice Eamon confirmed the typical circumstances attracting solicitor-client costs (maintaining the citations referenced by Eamon J): [47] In Sidorsky [Sidorsky v CFCN Communications Limited, 1997 ABCA 280], the Court provided the following examples of rare cases when an award of reasonably incurred solicitor and client costs could be justified: [28] Costs are discretionary and as a general rule, a departure from party and party costs should only occur in rare and exceptional circumstances.
Examples of such circumstances, outlined in Jackson v.
Trimac Industries Ltd.

(1993), 1993 CanLII 7031 (AB KB), 138 AR 161 at 172 (QB), include: 1. circumstances constituting blameworthiness in the conduct of the litigation by that party (Reese et al v Alberta (Minister of Forestry, Lands and Wildlife) et al, 1992 CanLII 2825 …, [1992] AJ No 745, 5 Alta LR

(3d) 40 (QB)); 2. cases in which justice can only be done by a complete indemnification for costs (Foulis et al v Robinson; Gore Mutual Inc Co, Third Party, 1978 CanLII 1307…, [1978] OJ No 3596, 21 OR

(2d) 769 (CA)); 3. where there is evidence that the plaintiff did something to hinder, delay or confuse the litigation, where there was no serious issue of fact or law which required these lengthy, expensive proceedings, where the positively misconducting party was “contemptuous” of the aggrieved party in forcing that aggrieved party to exhaust legal proceedings to obtain that which was obviously his (Max Sonnenberg Inc v Stewart, Smith (Canada) Ltd, 1986 CanLII 1771…, [1986] AJ No 1036, 48 Alta LR

(2d) 367 (QB)); 4. an attempt to deceive the court and defeat justice, an attempt to delay, deceive and defeat justice, a requirement imposed on the plaintiff to prove facts that should have been admitted, thus prolonging the trial, unnecessary adjournments, concealing material documents from the plaintiffs and failing to produce material documents in a timely fashion (Olson v New Home Certification Program of Alberta, 1986 CanLII 1640 …, [1986] AJ No 347, 44 Alta LR

(2d) 207 (QB)); 5. where the defendants were guilty of positive misconduct, where others should be deterred from like conduct and the defendants should be penalized beyond the ordinary order of costs (Dusik v Newton
(1984), 51 BCLR 217, 1984 CanLII 690 …; 6. defendants found to be acting fraudulently and in breach of trust (Davis v Davis, 1981 CanLII 3545 …, [1981] MJ No 320, 9 Man R

(2d) 236 (QB); 7. the defendants' fraudulent conduct in inducing a breach of contract and in presenting a deceptive statement of accounts to the court at trial (Kepic v Tecumseh Road Builder et al, [1987] OJ No 890, 23 OAC 72); 8. fraudulent conduct (Sturrock v Ancona Petroleums Ltd, 1990 CanLII 5563 …, [1990] AJ No 738, 111 AR 86 (QB)); and 9. an attempt to delay or hinder proceedings, an attempt to deceive or defeat justice, fraud or untrue or scandalous charges (Pharand Ski Corp v Alberta, 1991 CanLII 5931 …, [1991] AJ No 902, 83 Alta LR
See also FIC Real Estate Fund v Phoenix Land Ventures, 2016 ABCA 303 at para 4; Prevatt v Prevatt at para 27.
[39] While costs in estate litigation are being drawn into alignment with costs in other civil litigation contexts (see, e.g., Foote Estate (Re), 2010 ABQB 197, Graesser J at paras 16-19
Babchuk v Kutz, 2007 ABQB 81 and Petrowski v Petrowski Estate, 2009 ABQB 753, Moen J
Salter v Salter Estate, 2009 CanLII 28403, 50 ETR

(3d) 227 (ONSC), Brown J, as he then was, at para 5), historically, courts in estate litigation cases countenanced solicitor-client costs payable from the estate not only for personal representative and successful parties, but unsuccessful parties: BA Schnurr and SB Tator, Estate Litigation, 2nd ed (Westlaw), § 19:2.

(b) Not Pre-Litigation Conduct Alone [40] Justice Eamon followed the list of circumstances attracting solicitor-client costs in AGS v RNS with an important qualification, at para 48: [48] The Court must not base an award of solicitor-client costs on pre-litigation conduct alone, independent of other circumstances (Pillar Resource Services Inc v PrimeWest Energy Inc, 2017 ABCA 19 at para 1 - 10, 153, 158
Weatherford Canada Partnership v Artemis Kautschuk und Kunstoff-Technik GmbH, 2019 ABCA 92 at para 14
Breen v Foremost Industries Ltd, 2024 ABKB 9 at para 11-12, 22 and authorities cited therein).
(c) Fiduciaries [41] A qualification to the no-pre-litigation-conduct qualification is that violations of duties by trustees or fiduciaries may attract solicitor-client costs.
See Polar Ice Express Inc v Arctic Glacier Inc, 2009 ABCA 20 at para 21 (“[t]rusts or a fiduciary relationship might be an exception”)
Evans v The Sports Corporation, 2011 ABQB 616, Graesser J at para 17, app dismissed 2013 ABCA 14
Lakusta Estate, 2010 ABQB 275, Hughes J, as she then was, at para 16
Bukkems Estate (Re), 2014 ABQB 678, Shelley J at para 10
Hrycyna v Hood, 2019 SKCA 30 at para 62
Siemens v Bawolin, 2002 SKCA 84 at paras 120-121.
[42] However, a yet further refinement is that a proven breach of fiduciary duty does not in all cases attract solicitor-client costs.

See Evans v The Sports Corporation at para 35(QB): “The Courts have not created any presumptions that breaches of trust or breaches of fiduciary duty should result in solicitor and client costs being awarded,” and para 58(QB).
Breaches of fiduciary duty, like other violations of legal duties, occur across a spectrum of seriousness.
Only breaches of fiduciary duty tending toward the more serious pole of the spectrum attract solicitor-client costs.
See, e.g., HSBC Bank Canada v 1100336 Alberta Ltd.
(Incredible Electronics Wholesale), 2012 ABQB 27, Marshall J at para 17; HSBC Bank Canada v Lourenco, 2012 ABQB 648, Goss J at paras 62-64, 66-67.
I find the comments of Justice Mainella in Re Parkinson Estate, 2024 MBCA 52 at paras 117-120 to be illuminating: [117] My view is consistent with the historical context.

Estate litigation has long drawn a distinction in costs awards between cases where the estate maladministration was due to inadvertence, lack of knowledge or poor judgment as compared to more egregious cases involving self-benefit, dishonesty or gross negligence (see Carmen S Thériault, ed, Widdifield on Executors and Trustees, 6th ed (Toronto: Thomson Reuters, 2024) (loose-leaf updated 2024, release 2) vol 1, ch 4 at 82.2-90 [Widdifield on Executors]).

[118] Additionally, in situations involving a breach of a fiduciary duty outside of an estate context, reprehensible, scandalous or outrageous conduct by a fiduciary has been accepted to be an appropriate reason to consider pre-litigation conduct in awarding costs (see Winnipeg (City) v Sheegl, 2023 MBCA 63 at para 140
Hrycyna v Hood, 2019 SKCA 30 at para 67
Siemens v Bawolin, 2002 SKCA 84 at paras 120-21).
The law should be harmonized in the same way in the context of estates.

[119] I see no compelling legal reason to require a court to overlook what may be important context in fashioning a costs award where a fiduciary has come up far short in meeting the stringent obligations the law expects.

As Dubin JA (as he then was) explained in Foulis v Robinson, 1978 CarswellOnt 466 at para 20, 1978 CanLII 1307 (ONCA), there are cases “in which justice can only be done by a complete indemnification for costs”.

In the right set of circumstances, an award of solicitor and client costs based on a trustee's pre-litigation conduct is entirely in keeping with the court's supervisory role to ensure that estates are not unwarrantedly depleted and to guarantee the integrity of fiduciary relationships.
[120] The respondent's reliance on the Court's comments in Dalrymple v DeMeyer Estate, 2022 MBQB 31 at para 31 [Dalrymple], is not persuasive as that case is distinguishable.
In Dalrymple, the Court found that the executors' conduct did not meet the high threshold of reprehensible, scandalous or outrageous conduct.

The Court did not in any way suggest that if the executors' conduct had met that high threshold, that would not be a factor that could be considered in fixing costs pursuant to r 57.01 of the KB Rules.

Enhanced Costs and Percentage of Solicitor-Client Costs [43] A practical problem is that between cases warranting indemnity through reasonable solicitor-client costs and cases whose costs can be settled by reference to the Schedule C tariff without alteration lies a broad range of cases involving many differing factors relevant to costs.
The principle of proportionality would suggest that indemnification beyond the Schedule C tariff may be appropriate for some of these cases.
How are proportional costs to be secured?

(a) Enhanced Schedule C Costs [44] If the facially applicable tariff is inadequate in the litigation and pre-litigation (if applicable) circumstances, one method of achieving proportional costs is through awarding “enhanced costs” by modifying Schedule C costs: see Serinus Energy at para 16.
Rules 10.31(1) and (3) and the authorities expressly authorize an array of tools or mechanisms for arriving at a reasonable costs award.

Justice Shelley wrote in Weatherford Canada Partnership v Addie, 2018 ABQB 571, affd 2019 ABCA 92 at para 55 (QB) that “Alberta courts have recognized that when Schedule C fees are inadequate, courts may use several different methods for determining appropriate costs, including the application of multipliers to a column, extra lump sums, or some fraction of solicitor-client costs ….” See also Ed Miller Sales & Rentals Ltd v Caterpillar Tractor Co, 1998 ABCA 118 at para 4.
(b) Percentage of Solicitor-Client Costs [45] Another method of measuring proportional costs is through an award of costs representing a percentage of reasonable solicitor-client costs.
This costs measure has a long history in Alberta civil litigation but was revisited in McAllister.

[46] The Court of Appeal has confirmed that in this costs context, as in the context of full recovery of solicitor-client costs, the costs at issue are solicitor-client costs, not costs set by the successful party's contractual obligation to pay its counsel's account, not the quantum of fees charged by counsel and paid by the successful party: Barkwell 1 at paras 55, 56.
Rather, the multiplicand solicitor and client costs are the amounts that might reasonably be paid for the successful party's legal services: Barkwell 1 at para 56
Kantor v Kantor at para 13 (taking into account the factors in r 10.2)
AGS v RNS at para 36.
Further, the percentage of fees to be paid cannot be disproportionate to, e.g., the issues and amounts of the litigation: Barkwell 1 at para 57
VLM v Dominey Estate at para 8. “The issue is not simply how much the successful party spent, but how much that party can reasonably expect the other party to pay ….
The costs awarded must be proportionate to the amounts in issue:” Barkwell 2 at para 74
VLM v Dominey Estate at para 8 (“The issue is … what amount the unsuccessful party can fairly be expected to contribute”)
AGS v RNS at para 37
Sutherland v Sutherland, 2023 ABCA 185 at para 4.

[47] In contrast to the full recovery of solicitor-client costs cases, the guideline or general level of partial indemnity is in the 40 - 50% range, keeping in mind that indemnification may be greater or lesser than this guideline: McAllister at paras 41-51.
[48] One might say that our Courts have recognized implicitly and in practice an indemnity subprinciple, falling under the broader principle of proportionality.
See the Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, RRO 1990, Reg 194, r 57.01(1) (0.a): 57.01

(1) In exercising its discretion under section 131 of the Courts of Justice Act to award costs, the court may consider, in addition to the result in the proceeding and any offer to settle or to contribute made in writing, (0.a) the principle of indemnity, including, where applicable, the experience of the lawyer for the party entitled to the costs as well as the rates charged and the hours spent by that lawyer ….

(i) Circumstances Attracting Percentage of Solicitor-Client Costs [49] Costs set at a percentage indemnity of reasonable solicitor-client costs do not require proof of the typical factors supporting full indemnity of reasonable solicitor-client costs: McAllister at para 50 (were those factors established, a successful party would doubtless prefer full to partial indemnity).
[50] In what circumstances may costs be set at a percentage of reasonable solicitor-client costs?

I refer to GO Community Centre at paras 148-150: [148] Historically, the percentage indemnity approach has been associated with lengthy, complicated litigation: Ed Miller at para 7 (“The suit was extraordinarily long ….
And it is believed to have been the longest completed civil trial in Alberta history”) and para 12 (“Another factor is the seriousness of the suit.
The amounts were enormous, the charges were grave, and the business implications considerable.
If ever there was a suit which did not call for penny-pinching half measures by the defendant, this was it”) ….

[149] The percentage indemnity approach has more recently been applied in less lengthy but nevertheless (to my eye) complex or at least moderately complex litigation, cases found perhaps part-way on the continuum between “the common stream of cases” and Ed Miller-style trials: Styles [Styles v Caravan Trailer Lodges of Alberta Limited, 2019 ABQB 558, Jones J]
Remington [Remington v Crystal Creek Homes Inc, 2018 ABQB 644, Jones J]
Athabasca Minerals [Athabasca Minerals Inc v Syncrude Canada Ltd, 2018 ABQB 551, Jones J] (five days allocated to reading time: at para 28)
Estate of Montgomery, 2019 ABQB 833, DB Nixon J [as he then was]

Intact Insurance [Intact Insurance Company v Clauson Cold & Cooler Ltd, 2019 ABQB 225, Dilts J] at paras 17-20; see Orbis Engineering [Orbis Engineering Field Services v Taifa Engineering Ltd, 2019 ABQB 592, Mah J] at para 12.
[150] An important feature of the cases to which the percentage indemnity approach has been extended is that the parties were sophisticated and similarly situated economically.
One does not hold surplus power.
There is not a “significant imbalance in the power and means of the parties;” “the playing field is level:” Styles at para 59; see Remington at paras 31, 33-35, 42.
Both, then, can be expected to face similar types of legal accounts.
Both are proceeding with knowledge of what the litigation is costing: Remington at para 29; Athabasca Minerals at para 65; Blough v Busy Music Inc, 2020 ABQB 19, Jones J at para 29.

Serinus Energy at para 55.

[51] On this last point, again one might suggest that a subprinciple concerning the parties' “reasonable expectations” is at work, as in Ontario r 57.01(1)(0.b), “the amount of costs that an unsuccessful party could reasonably expect to pay in relation to the step in the proceeding for which costs are being fixed.” [emphasis added] See Barkwell 1 at para 59: [59] Further, if the trial judge decides to make a costs award based on a percentage of solicitor and client costs the analysis must go further.

The question is not just whether the solicitor and client costs are reasonable as between solicitor and client, but whether the quantum represents an amount that the losing party in the litigation should reasonably be expected to pay to the winning party ….

[emphasis added] [52] McAllister itself concerned an almost completed piece of protracted litigation, which included a trial, and the many steps required to bring the matter to trial and involved “arguably novel liability” (paras 1, 64).

(ii) Setting Costs at a Percentage of Solicitor-Client Costs [53] “[T]here is no presumption in the Rules that the successful party is entitled to any particular level of indemnification:” VLM v Dominey Estate at para 6.
A successful party seeking percentage indemnity costs must show that this is the appropriate measure of costs.

[54] The Court of Appeal stated in Barkwell 1 at para 60 that [60] If the winning party seeks a costs award based on a percentage of solicitor and client fees, that request must be justified by a consideration of the factors in r 10.2 that are relevant to the reasonableness of a fee.
That includes the importance of the issues, the circumstances of the client, the manner in which the services were provided, the skill and responsibility involved, and other relevant considerations.
Many of those same issues are also listed in r 10.33, which in addition to the amount in issue, refers to the complexity of the action and the conduct of the parties.

Also relevant are things like the hourly rates being charged (including paralegal or administrative time), whether those rates were appropriate given the seniority and experience of counsel, whether the work was being done by lawyers of appropriate seniority, the number of counsel involved, whether the duration and intensity of pre-trial questioning was appropriate or excessive or disproportionate, whether unnecessary interlocutory proceedings were launched and the outcome of those proceedings, and whether the ultimate fee was proportionate to the issues.
See also McAllister at para 46; Ho v Lau, 2023 ABKB 15, Lema J at para 42.

Schedule C Costs [55] Costs are often awarded by reference to Schedule C to the rules. “Using Schedule C has the advantage of providing parties with greater certainty as to their exposure to costs, it is simple, efficient, and inexpensive to apply, and in many cases avoids the need for lengthy inquiries into and assessment of the appropriate level of costs: McAllister at paras 59-60, 62:” Barkwell 1 at para 53: VLM v Dominey Estate at para 5
AGS v RNS at para 38.
In many cases Schedule C represents an appropriate level of indemnification: VLM v Dominey Estate at para 6.

[56] Schedule C to the rules provides a rough measure of proportional costs, presupposing notional reasonable legal fees (the costs that should reasonably have been incurred given the issues), using the amount of claims as a proxy for more granular r 10.33 considerations, and setting specific amounts that are in effect 40-50% of the notional reasonable legal fees: see McAllister at para 37
Barkwell 1 at paras 57, 58
VLM v Dominey Estate at para 6
Serinus Energy at para 26.
Schedule C costs may be refined by consideration of the r 10.33 factors (r 10.31(3)(b)).
[57] As indicated, Schedule C costs may be “enhanced” by various techniques to bring a costs award into line with proportional costs.

The first principle is that the successful party is presumptively entitled to costs, and that those costs are payable forthwith: R.

Special reasons are generally required to deny a successful party its costs, and very unusual reasons are required to justify having the successful party actually pay costs: Kretschmer v Terrigno, 2012 ABCA 345 (CanLII) at paras.
[22] The second principle is that a party can be denied “wasted” costs, such as costs which arise from that party's own carelessness, misconduct or default: R.

This situation can apply when a party applies to withdraw an admission that was improvidently made, to open up a noting in default, to amend defective pleadings, or where it must apply to repeat a procedural step because of self-generated deficiencies: see David M.
Gottlieb Professional Corp. v Nahal, 2013 ABCA 154 (CanLII) at para.
A particular manifestation of this principle is found in R.
(1) Subject to subrule
(2), the costs, if any, as a result of an amendment to a pleading are to be borne by the party filing the amendment unless
(a) the amendment is a response to an amended pleading, or
(b) the Court otherwise orders.
(2) The costs of a contested application to amend a pleading are in the discretion of the Court, in accordance with rule 10.29 [General rule for payment of litigation costs].
While this rule creates a presumption that the amending party must bear the costs of the amendment, it is not absolute.
The judge's wide discretion over costs is maintained both in R.
3.66(1)(b) with respect to amendments generally, and R.
3.66(2) with respect to contested amendments.
[23] The third principle is that costs should not provide a complete indemnity.
This is to ensure that parties only take procedural steps that are proportionate to the issues involved, the possible remedies, and any prejudice that may result.
If parties were entitled to indemnity costs every time they were successful, there would be an incentive towards “scorched earth” litigation.

Any time an applicant sought relief that resulted in whole or in part from its own default, the respondent might be tempted to fight to the end, even though the moving party could meet the test for the requested relief.
R.
3.66(2) reflects this principle, because it identifies as a special category contested amendment applications.

If a party applies to amend pleadings, and it seems that the amendment will likely be permitted, the respondent is not entitled to resist the amendment on the expectation that it will nevertheless receive costs under R.
