First, costs provide some compensation to a successful litigant.
The litigant is not required to shoulder alone all of the expense of legal vindication.
In that way, costs serve the higher order objective of enhancing access to justice by providing deferred reimbursement to a successful litigant.
This higher-order objective also imposes constraints on costs, which I'll return to below.
Second, costs promote rational and litigation norm-consistent decision making.
On the one hand, costs discourage frivolous claims and discourage improper litigation behaviour.
On the other hand, by adding a measure of predictable risk to litigation, costs can contribute to incentives for settlement.

They are awarded against tribunals in unusual or exceptional circumstances such as capricious or arbitrary conduct or a lack of good faith or circumstances otherwise contrary to rules of natural justice.

However, the Government of the day, in creating it as an instrument of government, gave it the power to sue and be sued.
Inherent in this power must be deemed to be the capacity to be awarded costs, or alternatively, to have costs awarded against it.
Otherwise, such a tribunal could engage in litigation, willy-nilly, without regard to the consequences, which would be judicially intolerable.
Indeed, the courts of this Province have recognized this principle, implicitly, by awarding costs on occasion, against such an administrative tribunal.
It has been recognized by these same courts, however, that, contrary to the normal practise, costs do not necessarily follow the event where administrative or quasi-judicial tribunals are concerned.

They may be awarded only in unusual or exceptional cases, and then only with caution. … I would conclude, on the basis of these few cases in which our courts have considered the matter, … that costs will not be, and should not be, awarded against such a tribunal, by reason only of a loss of jurisdiction on its part.

Where, however, that loss of jurisdiction resulted from conduct on the part of the tribunal which can be held to be capricious, arbitrary, lacking in good faith, or otherwise running contrary to the rules of natural justice, then unquestionably, costs should be awarded against it.
In addition to the above enumerated factors, there may well be others of the same or similar ilk which may result in an adverse award of costs.

Using a broad brush, it might be said that where the tribunal has acted in good faith and conscientiously throughout, albeit resulting in error, the reviewing tribunal will not ordinarily impose costs.
On the other hand, where these characteristics have not been clearly evident, the court will cast a caustic eye upon it which will normally result in costs being awarded against it.

This does not, of course, prevent the parties from reaching an agreement on this issue; indeed, the lawyer for the defendants indicated at the costs hearing that he would seriously present any reasonable proposal for paying costs over time to his clients.
In reaching the conclusion that courts should not give litigants time to pay court costs, I have relied on first principles and on analogy to other areas of civil practice.
The first factor to take into account in this analysis is that the impecuniosity, or lack of financial resources of a litigant, is no reason to shield that litigant from the full effect of costs.
Impecuniosity will mean, of course, that the party who has obtained the costs award, like a party who obtains a judgment, may not be able to recover the full amount of the award.
But the making of the award constitutes at least a moral victory for the person who obtains the benefit of the award, even if the award can never be enforced.
The second factor is that costs focus backwards, that is they relate to fees and expenditures which have already been paid or incurred.
Therefore, the person who is awarded costs is, as a matter of principle, entitled to the payment of those costs as soon as they are ordered.

There was a period during which this statement of principle would not have applied in Alberta to interlocutory matters; however, since Alberta has moved to a “pay as you go” basis for the payment of costs even on interlocutory matters, such costs are payable as soon as they as ordered.

This is particularly true, of course, in situations such as this one where the costs award is linked to a final decision in proceedings … The third factor to consider is the public policy which supports the making of final decisions in the court system.

This applies even to situations in which a substantive award is made, for example to a victim of a motor vehicle accident; that award may cover both damages or payments that have been made in the past as well as damages that may arise in the future.

A negligent driver is not entitled to make periodic payments to a successful plaintiff; the driver who has been found negligent has a legal obligation to pay the whole of the judgment immediately. … Even stronger policy considerations apply to costs awards: there is no comparable risk of over-compensation in costs awards because only past events influence the making of the award.
In this context, it is important to note that the relatively recent increases in Alberta's Schedule C tariff of costs recognize the reality of the high costs of the litigation process.

It costs litigants a lot of money to initiate, or defend, civil litigation; when a litigant is successful, it is only fair that the litigant should be re-imbursed in a timely way for some portion of those costs.

The last factor to be taken into account in determining whether the court should establish a schedule of payment for costs is the purpose of awarding costs: costs constitute the basis of discipline in the civil court process.

Delaying the payment of costs might tend to undermine the principle that costs which are paid when incurred keep the litigants in touch with the financial reality of litigation; this reality check should promote and nurture reasonable settlements.
It is true, of course, that in criminal proceedings, a convict may be given time to pay a fine and that time may be extended from time to time.

However, the practice in criminal proceedings is not comparable to the practice in civil proceedings because, in criminal matters, the ability of an offender to pay a fine is a matter which is relevant to the imposition of the penalty.
As indicated above, the impecuniosity of a litigant is not relevant to the issue of costs in a civil proceeding.

Moreover, it is important to notice that a fine is a form of retribution to the community at large; a convict who cannot afford to pay a fine can, instead, work off the fine by doing community service work.

In civil proceedings, an award of costs is not a punishment and is not imposed for the benefit of the community; it is a re-payment to a litigant of what have been found to be unnecessary expenses incurred for the purpose of the lawsuit.
In summary, therefore, there are many reasons of principle why a court should not deprive a litigant of the full and timely benefit of costs which have been awarded.

A Bullock order allows a plaintiff to add to the costs recoverable from an unsuccessful defendant the amount of costs which he is obliged to pay to a successful defendant: Griffin v City of Summerside, 2010 PECA 15, para 39, 299 Nfld & PEIR 119.

The rationale behind Bullock and Sanderson orders is explained by Mark Orkin, Law of Costs, 2d ed, vol 1 (Thomson Reuters, 1987) (loose-leaf, release 70, September 2017) 2–117: Where a plaintiff recovers judgment against one of several defendants and the action is dismissed against the others, in the normal course the plaintiff will be entitled to costs against the unsuccessful defendant, and the successful defendant will be entitled to costs against the plaintiff.

However, where the allocation of responsibility between defendants is uncertain, usually because of interwoven facts, it is often reasonable for a plaintiff to proceed through trial in order to establish liability.
In this situation the courts have devised two alternatives known respectively as a Bullock order and a Sanderson order.

Simply put, a Bullock order directs an unsuccessful defendant to reimburse the plaintiff for the coats of the successful defendant; a Sanderson order directs that the payment go directly to the successful defendant.
(See also Garrioch v Sonex Construction Ltd, 2017 ABCA 262, para 5, 60 Alta LR (6th) 51).

[71] The granting of a Sanderson or Bullock order in Alberta involves applying a tri-partite test; an applicant must show that “(a) it was reasonable for the plaintiff to join the successful defendant(s)
(b) there is no good reason to deprive the successful defendant of his costs, and

(c) the unsuccessful defendant was wholly responsible for the action”: Palechuk v Fahrlander, 2008 ABCA 10, para 5, [2008] 4 WWR 265, quoting from McLeod v Great Western Distributors Ltd, 1941 CanLII 408 (AB QB), [1941] 3 WWR 827, 829
Garrioch, para 6.

The Court went on to discuss the second and third parts of the three-part test: [73] The second requirement, no good reason to deprive the successful defendant of its costs, has been described as simply a judicial discretion to refuse a Sanderson or Bullock order in appropriate circumstances.

[76] This requirement serves the purpose of determining which type of order, Sanderson or Bullock is appropriate.

(6th) 95, Justice Yamuachi gave a history of Bullock and Sanderson costs orders, and then said this: 7 Courts in Alberta have made Bullock orders and Sanderson orders.

The test to determine whether a court should grant such an order was articulated by Perras J in Allen (Next friend of) v University Hospitals Board, 2000 ABQB 965 at para 6, 276 AR 345, where he said the following: The test is this: 1. was it reasonable for [the Plaintiff] to join the successful defendants given the circumstances; 2. is there any good reason to deprive the successful defendants of costs; and 3. were the unsuccessful defendants vis a vis the successful defendants wholly responsible for the action.
8 See also Palechuk v Fahrlander, 2008 ABCA 10 at para 5, citing McLeod v Great Western Distributors Ltd, [1941] 3 WWR 827 at 829.
9 The first part of the test has been referred to as a “threshold question.” See e.g.
Moore v Hayik (2008), 90 OR (3d) 463 at para 41 (CA).

In Bullock, Collins MR explained this threshold question as follows: [Permitting joinder of defendants] to a particular case does not arise upon proof of a joint or other wrong, but upon the state of mind of a plaintiff who does not know exactly whether an injury of which he complains arose from the joint act of two parties or the sole act of one or other of them.
Bullock at 271.

10 In Besterman v British Motor Cab Company Ltd[1914] 3 KB 181 at 186–87, Vaughan Williams LJ articulated the threshold question as follows: Under these circumstances, was it a reasonable thing for the plaintiff in this action against a man who ultimately turns out to be in fact the wrong-doer to join the other defendant in order that the matter might be thoroughly threshed out?

If, in the circumstances, it was a reasonable thing to do, then he was entitled to add as part of the costs in bringing this reasonable action in which he reasonably joined this other person the costs of that other person who is found not to be at fault.

11 The second part of the test could be extracted from Sanderson where Romer LJ said the following: Of course, in exercising the jurisdiction [to make this type of order for costs], a judge should have regard to the circumstances of the case, and be satisfied that it is just that the unsuccessful defendant should, either directly or indirectly, have to pay the costs of the successful defendant.

In the present case I do not think that I myself should have given to the defendant hope, having regard to his defences and conduct, any costs whatever, either as against the plaintiff or co-defendant.
Sanderson at 539.
12 Perras J described this part of the test as the discretion that courts exercise in determining whether to grant a Bullock order or a Sanderson order.

He said, “[i]t is my view that this stage of the test, as articulated in Alberta courts, ought to be viewed as providing a guide for the ‘judicial’ exercise of discretion rather than dictating it”: Allen at para 13.

13 In Gladue v Alberta (Attorney General), 2011 ABQB 535 at para 39, Veit J framed the 3-part test as follows: In Alberta, the courts have articulated a three stage test for determining whether a costs recovery order—either a Bullock or a Sanderson order—is appropriate: was it reasonable for the plaintiff to add the successful defendant to the litigation, was it reasonable for the plaintiff to keep the successful defendant in the litigation, and is it fair and just to require the unsuccessful defendant to pay the costs of the successful defendant. … Alberta's test makes it somewhat clearer that a litigant has an obligation to not only begin, but to maintain, reasonable conduct of litigation, and leaves the discretion of the judge who must determine costs untrammelled other than the usual obligation to exercise the discretion in a judicial way.
[Emphasis added].
14 It is this Court's view that the second 2 parts of the 3-part test to which Veit J referred are best considered under the second part, as Perras J articulated in Allen.
Why?
This is the part of the test in which the court exercises its discretion in making or not making a Sanderson order or a Bullock order.
It is the “equitable balancing” aspect of the test.

15 In Strategic Acquisition Corp v Multus Investment Corporation, 2017 ABQB 297 at para 84, Mahoney J said the following: In the absence of special circumstances, I decline to make a Sanderson or Bullock costs order.
[Strategic Acquisition Corp] as the party that initiated proceedings, must bear the primary risk of meeting Starke's costs against whom it was eventually unsuccessful.

The fact that the conduct of the defendants was related is in itself insufficient; such circumstances exist in most cases where more than one defendant is properly joined by a plaintiff … … 32 This Court agrees with Perras J's views on the third part of the test.

This Court, however, is of the view that the third part of the test should be expanded such that if the unsuccessful Defendant and the Plaintiffs were responsible for the action and maintaining the action against the successful Defendants, neither a Sanderson order nor a Bullock order is appropriate.
See e.g.
Garrioch v Sonex Construction Ltd, 2017 ABCA 262 at para 11.
As well, if the Plaintiffs themselves were responsible for the action and maintaining the action against the successful Defendants, those orders would not be appropriate.
The test set forth in Allen (Next friend of) v.
University Hospitals Board, 2000 ABQB 965, 2000 CarswellAlta 1542, (sub nom.
Allen v.
University Hospitals Board) 276 A.R.
345, as referred to by Justice Yamauchi in UBG Builders Inc., Re, 2017 ABQB 791, 2017 CarswellAlta 2893, 62 Alta.
L.R.
(6th) 95, was also applied by Kenny J. in O'Meara v.
Yule, 2004 ABQB 151, 355 A.R.
67, affirmed 2006 CarswellAlta 314, 2006 ABCA 86 at pp.
In Garrioch v.
Sonex Construction Ltd., 2017 ABCA 262, 2017 CarswellAlta 1755, a roll-over motor vehicle accident resulted in the five passengers in the vehicle being injured.
Sonex Construction owned the vehicle which had been operated by Tyler Tessman.
Four actions were commenced by the injured passengers against Tessman (represented by the Administrator of the Motor Vehicle Accident Claims Fund) and Sonex.
The allegation of the individual plaintiffs was that Tessman was operating the motor vehicle with the express or implied consent of Sonex.
That issue, common to the four actions, was directed to be tried.
The learned trial judge found Sonex liable, but that was overturned on appeal.

The Court of Appeal discussed Bullock and Sanderson orders for costs: [4] Sonex argues that the respondents should all be jointly liable for its costs, or that the Administrator should pay all the costs.

The Administrator argues that responsibility for the trial costs should be divided in thirds, with it and each of the two groups of plaintiffs paying one share, and that responsibility for the appeal costs should be divided in half, with it paying half, and the plaintiffs paying the other half.

The plaintiffs argue that the Administrator should pay all the costs, or in the alternative, there should be a Bullock order directing that the Administrator indemnify the plaintiffs for any portion of the costs they have to pay to Sonex.
[5] All of the parties have acknowledged the presumption that the successful party, Sonex, is entitled to its costs.

Where a plaintiff sues several defendants, but only succeeds against one, the partly successful plaintiff that is required to pay costs to the successful defendant may be entitled to an indemnity for those costs from the unsuccessful defendant (a Bullock order).
Sometimes the unsuccessful defendant is just ordered to pay directly all the costs of both the successful plaintiff and the successful defendant (a Sanderson order).
There is little practical difference between the two types of orders if all of the parties are solvent.
[6] The cases, such as Condominium Corp.
No.
9813678 v Statesman Corp., 2012 ABCA 265 (CanLII) at para.
15, 74 Alta LR (5th) 301, 536 AR 213, and Wainwright (Town) v 876947 Ontario Ltd., 2010 ABCA 23 (CanLII) at para.
19, 18 Alta LR
(5th) 21, 469 AR 383 identify the factors to be considered before making a Bullock order, which include:
(i) that it was reasonable for the plaintiff to join the successful defendant
(ii) that there is no good reason to deprive the successful defendant of its costs; and
(iii) as between co-defendants, the unsuccessful defendant was responsible for the action.
As this statement of the test anticipates, a Bullock or Sanderson order is commonly (but not exclusively) called for where the defendants mount “cutthroat defences”.
This occurs where it is reasonable for the plaintiff to sue a number of potential defendants, because liability is unclear.
Each defendant points to the other as being primarily or solely responsible.
At the end of the day, the unsuccessful defendant (or the one who is found to be primarily responsible) may be called upon to pay the plaintiff's and successful defendant's costs.

Even if the other defendant bore some minor responsibility for the damage caused, that defendant might not be called upon to contribute to the plaintiff's costs, and might even be indemnified for its own costs.
Impecuniosity and Sanderson and Bullock orders In UBG Builders Inc., Re, 2017 ABQB 791, 2017 CarswellAlta 2893, 62 Alta.
L.R.
(6th) 95, Justice Yamauchi discussed how a court should consider a party's impecuniosity in a determination of who should pay costs.
His Lordship said: 27 Should this Court consider Valour Park's impecuniosity when it makes a determination as to which party will bear the costs?
It is a factor that this Court must take into account when it makes its costs award.

In 1483677 Ontario Ltd v Crain, 2010 ONSC 1353 at para 24, Himel J said, “[i]n deciding whether to grant a Bullock or Sanderson order, the risk of not recovering is a determining factor.”[Emphasis added].

In Widdis (Litigation Guardian of) v Hall (1995), 22 OR (3d) 187 at 189 (Ct Jus (Gen Div)), Misener J said the following: The prima facie rule is that the successful Defendant is therefore entitled to look to the Plaintiff for its costs.

A Sanderson Order relieving the Plaintiff from that obligation and imposing it directly on the unsuccessful Defendant should not be made if there is a real risk that the successful Defendant will not receive those costs from the unsuccessful Defendant because of the latter's impecuniosity.
That real risk certainly exists in this case.
Accordingly, the prima facie rule must prevail … [Emphasis added].
See also Craven v Chmura, 2015 ONSC 4843 at para 9.
28 Erb J took a similar approach in Archer v St John, 2008 ABQB 245 at para 26, where she said the following: There is no evidence before me that the Defendant, Laureen St.
John, is impecunious.
Nevertheless, a balancing of equities leads me to conclude that any risk of non-recovery of costs from Ms.
St.
John should be borne by the Plaintiff, Devon Archer, rather than Mountain View Credit Union and the Estate of Gerald Archer.
[Emphasis added].
29 In Archer, Erb J referred to the “risk of non-recovery,” which requires the plaintiff to undertake a risk assessment when commencing and conducting litigation.

In Rowe v Investors Syndicate Ltd (1984), 46 CPC 209 at 271 (Ont H Ct Jus), Henry J explained this risk assessment as follows: The equitable issue is whether the plaintiffs or [the successful defendant] should bear the risk of non-recovery.
A “Bullock” order will prejudice the plaintiffs, a “Sanderson” order the successful defendant.
As between the two equity lies with the [successful] defendant.
The plaintiffs took the risk of bringing [the successful defendant] to Court and did not succeed.
See also SGH v Gorsline, 2001 ABQB 671 at para 21.
30 Because Valour Park is impecunious, a Sanderson order places the risk of non-recovery on the successful defendants.
The Plaintiffs, in the case at bar, took the risk that they might not be able to recover costs from Valour Park because of Valour Park's impecuniosity.
Although this Court does not see this as “the determining factor,” it is one factor that this Court must consider in weighing the balance.
See also Rowe at 214.

Costs in the Cause when Trial Does Not Occur The defendants say that because there was no trial, no costs for pre-trial procedures where costs were reserved for disposition by the trial judge can be awarded.
I disagree.
It was clearly the intention of the judges who decided the interlocutory motions that costs would be dealt with.
They did not say that there would be no costs for those procedures, or that there would be no costs in the event of settlement.
In the event, because there was a settlement, there was no trial of the substantive issues in the lawsuit.
However, the decision about who is to get what costs remains an issue to be determined.
It is appropriate that the judge who had been assigned to hear the trial should determine costs.
Lines v.
Brink (1994), 24 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 227 (Q.B.), at 234, per Veit J.
Costs on Appeal This is a special application, after the oral hearing, for an award of costs to the successful appellant for the original hearing in Queen's Bench.
These were not awarded at the oral hearing because no mention was made of them at that time.
Apparently, counsel assumed that our practice is that an award of costs to the successful appellant automatically includes a reversal of a costs award at trial.
It does not.
Our practice is, as the Practice Note of November 15, 1991 says, that costs of the appeal follow the event unless some special circumstances come to our attention.
Costs of trial must, on the other hand, be sought in the factum and at the oral hearing, or the court might refuse to award them on that ground alone.
We treat the present application as, first, leave to reargue the costs issue, and make a request for trial costs.
We would grant the leave because of the mistake, and because no harm came from it other than the need, and nuisance, for this application.
We are not likely to take that view in the future, now that this case removes any doubt about our practice.
West Edmonton Mall Ltd. v.
McDonald's Restaurants of Canada Ltd.
76 (C.A.), at 77, per the court.
The Practice Note referred to by the Court of Appeal is Court of Appeal Practice Note H—Costs in Civil Matters, and is reproduced in App.
IV, infra.
In Hogarth v.
Rocky Mountain Slate Inc., 2013 ABCA 116, 2013 CarswellAlta 835, 87 Alta.
L.R.
(5th) 108, the Court said, in relation to costs awards made at appeal, at paragraph 12: 12 On appeal, the appellant Simonson was successful in having the entire judgment against him set aside.
As such, he is entitled to assessed costs of the appeal.
The respondents argue that Simonson should not receive full, or any costs, because he was not successful on all of the arguments that he raised.
Costs, however, are not usually allocated on an issue by issue basis: Mahe v.
Boulianne, 2010 ABCA 74, at para.
6, 21 Alta LR (5th) 277.

It is rare for a litigant to be successful on each and every issue, but that does not mean that litigants should not argue every issue reasonably raised on the record, nor does that disentitle them to costs.
At the end of the day Simonson was successful on appeal in having the entire judgment set aside, and he is entitled to costs.
Successful Appeal Usually Overrides Costs Awarded at Trial In Ed Miller Sales & Rentals Ltd. v.
Caterpillar Tractor Co., [1996] 9 W.W.R.
449 (Alta.
C.A.), this Court held that where the appellant succeeded entirely on appeal, there was no longer any basis for the award of costs at trial. . . . . .
The general rule is that costs are awarded throughout to the successful party on appeal.

Nonetheless, the Court may choose not to disturb an award of costs at trial in favour of a losing party in a case involving special and peculiar problems, where, for example, an act of the state has compelled a response to protect preceived rights concerning a constitutional matter of fundamental importance.
Public School Boards' Assn.
(Alberta) v.
Alberta (Attorney General) (1998), 64 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 390 (C.A.), at 395–96, per curiam, [additional reasons to (1998), 60 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 62 C.A.; leave to appeal allowed (1998), 235 N.R.
395n S.C.C.; leave to appeal refused (1999), 237 A.R.
Appeals from Applications Judge In 1808882 Alberta Ltd. v.

Moderno Ventures Ltd., 2018 ABQB 1000, 2018 CarswellAlta 2993, Justice Eamon noted that while a party appealing an order granted by a Master was allowed to produce evidence not put before the Master, there can be costs consequences if it is found that the late production of the evidence resulted in a waste of time.
His Lordship said: [12] I also take into account the Appellant's conduct of the summary judgment proceedings.
Appeals from Masters' decisions are de novo and a party is permitted to add evidence and arguments on appeal.
That does not mean there are no costs consequences for failing to efficiently conduct the proceedings.

As I said in my appeal reasons, [71]… Where decisive additional evidence or a new argument is adduced on appeal, any prejudice can be addressed by penalizing the successful appellant in costs for wasting the application before the Master where appropriate.

Of course, other considerations might also factor into that decision such as litigation misconduct by the other side, time pressures in the proceeding below such as those often seen in assembling evidence or responding in the context of a morning chambers list, or the like.
[13] I agree with Master Prowse QC that the Plaintiff 180's evidence on the application in Master's Chambers was wholly inadequate.

Also, the Plaintiff 180 wanted to cross-examine on the Defendant's affidavit, but was unable to arrange it and made a strategic decision to proceed in Master's Chambers without it (Transcript, May 2, 2018, pp 30–31).
On appeal, the Appellant conducted the cross-examination which it earlier decided to forego and added substantial new evidence to the appeal record including that testimony.
[14] The Appellant's approach to summary judgment was akin to litigation by instalment, starting from an obviously weak position before the learned Master and curing the gaps on appeal.
That conduct unreasonably and unnecessarily delayed the litigation and increased cost and effort.

Although the Appellant has already borne adverse costs consequences for its failure in the initial application, its costs award on the appeal should be reduced to address the prejudice of delay and wasted effort associated with its approach and encourage parties to reasonably prepare summary judgment applications by placing the necessary record before the Master.
The same approach was taken by Justice Hollins in Prestige Granite & Marble Inc. v.

Maillot Homes Inc., 2018 ABQB 1040: [23] On that point, I am in agreement with the approach of my brother, Justice Eamon, who in a recent case in which an appellant relied on new evidence not presented to the Master, deprived the appellant of part of its costs, notwithstanding its success on appeal; 1808882 Alberta Ltd v Moderno Ventures Ltd.
2018 ABQB 1000 (CanLII).
Justice Mah, in Alberta Finance & Mortgage Corp. v Bruce Steel Erectors Ltd., 2018 ABQB 907 (CanLII) has done likewise.
Rule 10.33(2) provides a menu of considerations for this Court on costs, including steps taken which have unnecessarily delayed the action.

In this case, while the Plaintiff successfully appealed the Master's Order, all that has really happened is that the parties have now exchanged the evidence necessary to allow them to resolve matters or properly prepare for trial.
See also: Rudichuk v.
Genesis Land Development Corp., 2019 ABQB 133, 2019 CarswellAlta 339 at paragraph 56.
Costs on Third Party Proceedings In Condominium Corporation 052 0580 (o/a The Tradition at Southbrook) v.

Carrington Holdings Ltd., 2024 ABKB 55, Justice Mandziuk referred to a situation in which an unsuccessful plaintiff should pay the costs of a third party: [33] The Plaintiff's action was dismissed in the Delay Application.
The Plaintiff did not directly sue the Third Parties, but they were brought in because of the Plaintiff's claim.
They incurred costs as a result.
The Third Parties faced liability, and they took steps in response to the Plaintiff's action which has now been dismissed.
[34] Weatherall v Seaba, 2009 ABQB 173 sets out situations where the Plaintiff should, in fairness, pay the costs of third parties.

One such situation is “where the third party proceedings follow naturally and inevitably upon the institution of the Plaintiff's action, in the sense that the defendant had no real alternative but to join the third party” (at para 16).
[35] The work of a developer is undertaken by an array of contracted parties.
Here, the Plaintiff sued the developer, and it flows naturally that the developer would have joined the myriad of sub-contractors which the Third Parties comprise.
I am satisfied that the Defendant's decision to bring the Third Parties into this action was inevitable upon the initiation of the action by the Plaintiffs.
When Does The Rule Apply?
In Chernetz v.
Eagle Copters Ltd.
L.R.
(4th) 297 (Q.B.), McMahon J., at p.
300, noted that “[t]he rule does not define ‘unsuccessful’.” After discussing whether “substantial success” was sufficient to engage the rule, his Lordship concluded, at p.
300, that: In respect of the production of documents and claims to privilege, it is my view that the substantial success test is not adequate.
It is not enough to be mostly or substantially correct to win costs. … To put it briefly, he who claims privilege had best be right if he wishes costs.
